utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Case IT-04-82-PT, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber would like to know from you whether you are following the proceedings in a language that you can understand. In other words, whether you are receiving interpretation in your own language. Make sure that the channel is the right one because otherwise, they wouldn't be receiving interpretation. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] It is all right. I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't answer my question. I want also a confirmation that you are receiving interpretation in your language. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, I can receive the interpretation in Macedonian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Mr. Tarculovski, same question to you. The Trial Chamber would like to know if you are receiving interpretation in your own language. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, I do receive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have appearances now. Appearances for the Prosecution, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. Kenneth Scott for the Office of the Prosecutor. I am joined this morning by Mr. Bill Smith, trial attorney, and our case manager Mr. Hasan Younis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Dragan Godzo, assisted by Kiril Waite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for Mr. Tarculovski. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Antonio Apostolski, attorney. I'm representing the accused Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you too. I notice -- or at least, I have been informed but I also see presence in the courtroom of representation from the government of the former Yugoslavia of Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Could you please identify yourselves for the record. Any one of you may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MLADENOVSKA-GJORGJIVESKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, representative of the government of the Republic of Macedonia is the Minister of Justice, myself, Meri Mladenovska-Gjorgjiveska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, madam, and welcome to this Tribunal. I also want to make sure that you are receiving interpretation in your own language, and that -- for that purpose I just draw your attention that if at any moment in the course of the proceedings there are problems with the interpretation that you are receiving in one way or another, please draw our attention straight away so that we will rectify it. Yes. But I do notice, Minister, that you are accompanied also by two other persons. Could I also have the names of the two persons that are accompanying you, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MLADENOVSKA-GJORGJIVESKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, members of the delegation are Biljana Micevska-Josifovska, advisor for international cooperation within the cabinet of the minister of justice, and Mr. Todor Mirovski, first secretary in the embassy of the Republic of Macedonia in The Hague, Kingdom of the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So this is a special hearing that we have decided to convene, having read -- having gone through the documents pertaining to the motion for provisional release, two different motions, and it's a hearing that we have convened to deal with some of the outstanding matters arising out of the motions and the relative responses. For the record, I only need to mention that Mr. -- accused Tarculovski filed his motion for provisional release on the 20th of May of this year, while Mr. Boskoski filed his on the 25th of May. Then the Prosecution filed responses on the 2nd and on the 7th of June respectively. Then subsequent to that, the Trial Chamber granted leave to the Defence to file -- to both accused to file their respective reply, which they both did on the 27th of June. After that, having gone through the documents, as I said, we came to the conclusion that it would be -- it would serve the purposes of justice better if we had -- if we gave a hearing. Today's oral submissions need not be very long. We are not going to ask you to repeat most of the submissions that we have already, and in any case, each party, and that includes you, Honourable Minister, will have a maximum of 15 minutes to address the Trial Chamber. Of course, there will be a right to a short reply afterwards. One other thing that I wanted to ensure before we proceed any further is that there is no representation from Croatia, from the government of Croatia, at least that I have been informed of, and I would like a confirmation on that from the registrar. There is no representation. No formal representation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I've been informed by telephone by the consulate yesterday that the Croatian delegation -- that the Republic of Croatia will not be represented at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. So that goes on the record as well. And I would start with Defence counsel for Mr. Boskoski. I'll give you the floor, sir. Please restrict your submissions to a very brief resume of the grounds upon which you are seeking the provisional release of your client and the various issues that seem to be in contention between you and the Prosecution. Also, particularly in relation to why you seek -- why you seek the provisional release of your client to the former republic -- Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia while there are proceedings pending against your client in Croatia. All right. You have the floor, and you have 15 minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Honourable Judges, among all the issues that have been presented in the filings, I will select some of them to present the case for provisional release of Mr. Boskoski clearly and briefly in five headings. The first point I'd like to make concerns the character of the accused and his cooperation with the Prosecution and the Tribunal. Legal circumstances, unfortunately, did not allow Mr. Boskoski to express his comprehensible respect to the Tribunal and to demonstrate his commitment to international rule of law and to -- with his voluntary surrender. Regrettably, at the time the indictment has been communicated to him, the accused was in Pula Detention Unit, waiting for another case. Being indicted before this Tribunal, Mr. Boskoski did not in any way or shape legally confront his transferring to The Hague. On his initial appearance, he has without any time delay entered a plea and kindly asked the Trial Chamber for immediate possible commencement of the case. To support the Defence's claim that the accused is a trustworthy person, that if released he will appear for trial, we have submitted some recommendations concerning that he is a man of trust issued by relevant Macedonian politicians. In their personal statements, they have referred to the character of the accused, his peaceful solutions to political problems, his democratic attitude with political parties, and his cooperation with the Prosecution and the Tribunal. Their joint conclusion leave no doubt that the accused will pose no danger to any victims or witnesses and will appear for trial. And maybe the best description of his personality was given by former Macedonian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Slobodan Cashulev, attached to the reply which I'd like to quote in brief. "Ljube Boskoski is a God-fearing, church-going person, an honest and highly ethical man, a loving father and a loyal friend. He is, as God is my witness, a human being with capital H anyone would pray to have on his side in times of need." The second very important issue I want to reveal are the -- is the test of proportionality. Mr. Boskoski's charged with three counts under Article 3 of the Statute, violations of law and customs of war, for failure to punish. He is not charged as a direct perpetrator of a single offence but instead he is indirectly involved in this case. Having in mind that this Tribunal deals only with serious charges, the Defence would, however, like to note that the charges against the accused are at the lower bottom end of the scale. In this case, a long period of detention of the accused is not a suitable and necessary measure, and moreover, the jurisprudence of both the Tribunal and the European Court of Human Rights has emphasised that gravity of the charges cannot by itself serve to justify a long period of pre-trial detention on remand. The third heading in my submissions concerns the crucial question whether the accused, if released, will appear for trial. His background as a relevant Macedonian politician and his personal and family honour leave him no other option than to appear before this Tribunal whenever ordered to do so to face the charges. He is absolutely convinced in his innocence, and he has full respect to the honourable members of the Chamber. Released or not, it is a matter of his personal interest to face the charges, to stand before the Trial Chamber, and to prove his innocence in this case in his family name and on behalf of Republic of Macedonia whose minister he was during the events in question. Mr. President, Your Honours, let me briefly make an analysis of his statement. He expresses his utmost readiness to participate in the proceedings. He has offered his whole personal assets as a bail bond. He has indicated that he will abide by whatever restriction the Court may impose to him. He has agreed to freeze his political career until the termination of the case. And at the end of this heading, I'd like to underline his intention to continue his political career after the trial. To do so, it would be vital for his career first to face the charges and to appear at the trial before this Tribunal. Therefore, the submissions as mentioned above indicate no fear for the Trial Chamber that he might flee. Mr. President, that brings me to the fourth heading, which is addressed to witnesses' intimidation. First of all, there is no indication for the accused as a violent person at all, and he has no criminal record. From the time he was indicted and especially from the moment the supporting material has been disclosed to the Defence, there has been no single interference done with any witnesses or victims. Four years after the event has gone and there has not been a history of a single indication of threatening of witnesses in Macedonia. Moreover, the accused has not been charged as a direct perpetrator but he's charged upon superior responsibility doctrine for failure to punish, Article 7(3) of the Statute. He has no intention to interfere with witnesses or victims since that cannot improve his case at all. And vice versa; the Prosecution's case against him could not be in any way interfered by witnesses' intimidation since it is not primarily based on their testimonies but instead on documents. If released, and he prefers to be released in Macedonia, the accused has given the Trial Chamber personal guarantees, inter alia, for not attending any personal contacts with witnesses and victims and for not -- and for not visiting the village of Ljuboten, which, by the way, he has never in his life visited before. At the other hand, may I generalise concerns about witnesses' safety or confidence don't justify refusing provisional release. An existing danger needs to be identified. There has to be clear threat to the safety of witnesses which is linked to specific acts or conduct by the accused. That was the approach of this Tribunal in the Haradinaj case, Prlic, Cermak and Markac, Stanisic, Milutinovic and Delic case. In this case, the Prosecutor has failed to point to any act or conduct or statement of the accused which represent any threat to actual or potential witnesses in this case. At the end of this hearing, the Defence would like to underwrite that in Republic of Macedonia there is no previous history of witnesses' intimidation at all. The fifth and very important issue are the guarantees. It would be pretty fair to conclude that the entire political scene in Macedonia has provided recommendation for Mr. Boskoski that he would appear for trial when ordered to do so. Parliament majority has issued the official government guarantee, and the opposition parliamentary party -- party leaders have generally expressed their support by written statements attached to the reply. Mr. President, in this courtroom Macedonian minister for justice has personally attended to this hearing to support the guarantees and to present the attitude of Republic of Macedonia regarding this Tribunal. Macedonian government has with absolute efficiency so far clearly demonstrated its commitment to international rule of law and to the supremacy of the Tribunal over its institutions, and has acted accordingly. Therefore, we can conclude nothing else than to admit that Republic of Macedonia has been successfully cooperative with the Tribunal so its guarantees can be trusted. And finally to conclude, as the Trial Chamber has noted in previous cases, the time assessment is a relevant factor when determining upon question for provisional release. On traditional -- on the initial appearance, the accused Mr. Boskoski could not be promised a speedy trial. The expectation of a speedy trial is not a visible option for him. Since the trial in this case is unlikely to begin even next year, the length of a pre-trial detention presents an additional heavy burden on the accused as a measure disproportional to the level of the charges and may represent violations of Article 5 and 6 of the European Convention of Human Rights. Therefore, having in mind all the relevant material, the Defence would once again like to underwrite that this is a clear case for provisional release. Presented material leaves no doubt that if released the accused will certainly appear for trial when ordered to do so, and he will pose no danger to victims and witnesses at all. Therefore, we ask the Trial Chamber to grant the motion primarily in Macedonia, because the Macedonia is the crime scene of the event and Ljube Boskoski is Macedonian politician. Furthermore, he would have no objections if he could be released in Croatia as well. He is ready to face all the charges, even the charges in the Rashtanski Lozja case, which, by the way, is Macedonian case, and there is a legal [Realtime transcript read in error "little"] possibility that Macedonian government can restore its jurisdiction to that case to be tried before Macedonian courts. Mr. President, Your Honours, those were the submissions I'd like to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And, Mr. Scott, would you prefer to answer now or shall we proceed with receiving submissions from Mr. Apostolski?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: In the record there is a little mistake, I think. I didn't say there is a little possibility, I said there is a legal possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. All right. Okay. Okay. All right. Okay. Mr. Scott, shall we proceed with the submissions of Mr. Apostolski or would you like to reply to the submissions we've just heard now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, may it please the Court, Mr. Smith will be handling the argument this morning, and I think it's his preference -- it would be our preference to respond individually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, Mr. Smith, what I suggest then, if you are going to respond to the submissions that we've heard from counsel for Mr. Boskoski, I think it's the case of giving the floor first to the Honourable Minister of Macedonia to make -- to present her submissions with regard to guarantees in particular, because then of course you can address that aspect immediately, in other words, rather than having it postponed to later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands. I'm happy to do it either way, but I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, it's up to you. If you feel more comfortable dealing with the two cases one by one, then of course that's how it will be done, but I don't think it makes sense to do -- to proceed with your reply before we have heard the Honourable Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Minister, you have the floor, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MLADENOVSKA-GJORGJIVESKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my capacity as the representative of the government of the Republic of Macedonia, I wish to state before you that if the accused Mr. Ljube Boskoski and Mr. Johan Tarculovski are provisionally released, and if they reside in the Republic of Macedonia, the government of the Republic of Macedonia guarantees that it will undertake all measures and activities to ensure their presence at all summons issued by the Trial Chamber at all trial and pre-trial hearings. Expecting the -- from the distinguished Trial Chamber of The Hague Tribunal to be understanding and to permit the guarantee -- accept the guarantee of the Republic of Macedonia for provisional release of Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski, the government of the Republic of Macedonia guarantees, pursuant to Rule 65 testimony Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal, that it will fulfil the following conditions: The accused will appear at the trial if they are provisionally released, and they won't pose any threat for no victim, witness, or any other person. Aware of the significance and the need of existence of such body within the international community, the government of the Republic of Macedonia reiterates the political will for full cooperation with this Tribunal. The Republic of Macedonia joins the many states which have thus far supported the Tribunal in acting upon all cases that fall within the competence of this Court dealing with persons who perpetrated criminal offences subject to establishing the criminal responsibility before the Tribunal. Your Honour, the government of the Republic of Macedonia stresses that the accused before The Hague Tribunal, Mr. Ljube Boskoski and Mr. Johan Tarculovski, before this Court have the right to full legal aid in the course of the entire procedure until the final verdict is brought. Over the past period of time, the successful cooperation with the Tribunal has been evident with the Republic of Macedonia, and we believe it will continue in the forthcoming period. The state institutions in the Republic of Macedonia over the past period of time have continuously and timely acted upon all motions regarding the cases within the competence of the Tribunal, and for this assistance and information in relation of which assistance and information have been requested from the Republic of Macedonia. The competent institutions in the Republic of Macedonia with the highest degree of professionality has cooperated with the representatives of the International Court in relation to all cases in which the Tribunal has expressed interest. This practice, I have to stress, is a political orientation of the government of the Republic of Macedonia and remains valid over the forthcoming period. Your Honour, the government of the Republic of Macedonia assures the Tribunal that it has legislation and other measures and activities that it can undertake. Dealing in terms of legislation, I would mention the law on criminal procedure, the law on internal affairs, and we also have numerous secondary legislation items as well as other mechanisms and measures which allow her to act and undertake activities in accordance with the motions and orders of the Trial Chamber in order to secure permanent presence at the territory of the Republic of Macedonia of the accused, and by this provide the accessibility and the appearance before the International Court at any time upon a motion from the Trial Chamber, and also prevent any interference with the witnesses in the procedure. On the basis of the constitution of the Republic of Macedonia, the government guarantees the accused protection of life, personal safety, and protection of their property. We reiterate our decision to respect the conditions for provisional release for each of the accused prescribed by the Trial Chamber, and upon its motion, to undertake activities if the accused violate any of the conditions. The state bodies in the Republic of Macedonia have the capacity, have legal mechanisms and capability to fully respect the decision issued by the Trial Chamber of The Hague Tribunal in relation to the guarantee that the Republic of Macedonia has submitted. A priority for the government of the Republic of Macedonia is to successfully continue our cooperation with The Hague Tribunal. These two cases are not and cannot be a reason for the cooperation, successful cooperation and the good relations between the government of the Republic of Macedonia and the Hague Tribunal to be disrupted. It means that the government of the Republic of Macedonia will not permit and will prevent a potential violation of the order and will immediately inform the Trial Chamber if the persons infringe the provisions from the order of the Trial Chamber. I am presenting the position of the government, that it will respond and act positively upon any order of the Trial Chamber in relation to these two cases. The government of the Republic of Macedonia, after potential handing over of the persons, assures the Court that it possesses legislation in the Republic of Macedonia which is applicable at the entire territory of the state and at all times and for any citizen and that it has the capacity and capability to undertake all legal measures which provide for acting upon the motion of the Trial Chamber. With this, we present the position that neither persons subject to the guarantee nor other citizens, no other persons, cannot perpetrate an offence which won't be sanctioned, and for this The Hague Tribunal has been informed timely. I am now discussing the cases of the two accused. As it is known, the Republic of Macedonia has no law for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, but that in any moment in the current cooperation with the Hague Tribunal has -- the non-existence of a law was not an obstacle for action. On the contrary, with all the activities that the -- the governmental bodies had in Macedonia, they presented their preparedness to act, sending all the cases that were asked by the Republic of Macedonia, submitting all the information to which -- which -- for which an answer was asked from us. This means that the successful cooperation it is -- it is our interest to continue in the future in a manner that has been taking place so far. The Republic of Macedonia, with the acts chargeable under The Hague Tribunal, is -- has been faced for the first time after the 2001 conflict and in the acting with these cases we have no big experience. Out of those reasons I would like to assure you that it is our interest to act in accordance to all the requests and orders that will be issued by the Trial Chamber to the institutions in Macedonia. This is our interest. That will continue. Since the cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, as I previously said, is a priority with the government, at the moment we are in the process of Euro integration, in the process of reforms significant for our country, and it is our interest that all these activities in the process of the reforms and cooperation with The Hague Tribunal to continue also in the future. In the Macedonian public, the image of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia established with the Resolution 827 of 25th of May, 1993, is a positive one and is based upon the assurance that this Tribunal makes just judgements. Your Honour, accepting of the guarantees of the government of the Republic of Macedonia for provisional release of the accused Mr. Ljube Boskoski and Mr. Johan Tarculovski can contribute to the strengthening of the dignity of this Tribunal before the Macedonian public as a just body. I thank you for the opportunity to present my guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Minister. So I think you have the floor now. And then, Mr. Apostolski, you will have the floor and we can conclude. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At the outset I believe I have 15 minutes but I might take a few extra minutes in relation to Mr. Boskoski because there are some common issues that would apply for Mr. Tarculovski as well. Your Honour, Mr. Boskoski's application is strongly opposed by the Prosecution. As Your Honour is well aware, it is for the Defence to prove on the balance of probabilities that he will appear for trial, the accused will appear for trial, and will not interfere or present a danger to victim witnesses or any other person. In relation to the first matter, will Mr. Boskoski appear for trial, I note at the outset that in relation to the Prosecution's response to the Defence motion for provisional release, the Prosecution raised the issue of Mr. Boskoski's non-attendance before the Macedonian courts in relation to the other matter which he is in custody in Croatia for. In fact, what happened last year, Mr. Boskoski fled from Macedonia once he discovered that he was indicted and subject to legal proceedings in the Macedonian courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let me interrupt you here. This is strongly contested by Mr. Boskoski in his reply. He said that he left Macedonia regularly in a legal way to proceed to Croatia where he was then held, detained, and et cetera. But you're using the word "fled." He's contesting that as a fact. And if you are in a position to address it further, considering his reply, then please do. Otherwise, of course I will give you back the floor later to address this issue, which is important. All right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That is correct, Mr. Boskoski does have dual citizenship and can either live in Croatia or Macedonia. However, the Prosecution submits from some evidence that we put before you shortly that the reason for Mr. Boskoski fleeing Macedonia in early last year, in 2004, was because of the legal proceedings instigated against him by the Macedonian courts. Your Honours, in the Prosecution response you would see -- of the 7th of June, you would see a request where the Prosecution has asked the Macedonian government for a number of pieces of information relating to this provisional release hearing. At the time that the Prosecution filed their response, a reply had not been -- had not been received, but recently a reply has been received from the Macedonian government, and in fact the documents that relate to that reply I think have been distributed to you in the last few minutes. The documents have been provided to the Defence yesterday, and what the documents do is highlight whether or not Mr. Boskoski in the past, in relation to the other case that he's on trial for in Croatia, whether in fact he attempted to avoid the judicial proceedings there. If Your Honours would be mind to look at tab 6 of those documents, and perhaps if people could -- if the Court could press the "computer evidence" button on their screens in Sanction, and I have a summary translation of one of the documents that's been provided by the Macedonian government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Honourable Minister and her team needs maybe some assistance to make sure that -- they do have. You do have the screen the text in Macedonian and in English?

utterances.speaker: MS. MLADENOVSKA-GJORGJIVESKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, everything is all right. Thank you. Everything is all right. Thank you. Everything is all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the accused himself. Mr. Boskoski, can you see this on your screen, Mr. Boskoski? THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And, counsel, Mr. Godzo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We have now lost the signal in the booth. We don't have it on our screens any longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't either, so we need -- we need either to press "computer evidence" again, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: We have it on one computer here, Your Honour, but not on the other. Perhaps, Your Honour, if I briefly summarised the content of the document and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's happening here? Yes. We have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. This is just a summary translation and a more complete one will follow today. However, this document best illustrates what Mr. Boskoski's actions were in relation to the judicial proceedings that were issued against him last year. As Your Honours are aware from the papers, Mr. Boskoski is on trial in Croatia for the involvement in the killing of seven illegal immigrants in Macedonia on the 2nd of March, 2002. He and four others, three of them from the Ministry of Interior, are alleged to have executed these men for political gain, and that's the process against Mr. Boskoski at the moment in Croatia. These charges were first raised against Mr. Boskoski on the 30th of April, 2004. As you can see in paragraph 2, the main Prosecution office, on the basis of -- the criminal charges were raised against Mr. Boskoski on the basis of a request from the Prosecution office. On that date, a request for investigation on the 30th of April was delivered to the investigative judge in Skopje who is working on the case with the four other accused. On that same date, the committee, the parliamentary committee for the mandate and immunity matters in the Macedonian Assembly relating to immunity for the question of immunity for members of parliament agreed that the decision to continue the privilege of immunity against Mr. Boskoski would no longer exist and immunity was removed. On that same day, a summons was served on Mr. Boskoski to report to an investigative judge on the 1st of May, 2004, for those murder charges. The summons was received by Mr. Boskoski's lawyer, Mr. Stavre Dzikov, in the Hotel Ambassador in Skopje where Mr. Boskoski was holding a press conference on the very issue of whether or not his immunity should be lifted from prosecution. On the 1st of May, when Mr. Boskoski was due to appear at the investigating judge's office by law, the three lawyers appeared but not Mr. Boskoski. They told the investigative judge that Mr. Boskoski was not going to appear because of a procedural irregularity in the lifting of the accused's immunity. As Boskoski did not appear on that date, the investigative judge -- and I think there's a mistake there, it says the 30th of April, it must in fact be the 1st of May -- brought a decision to bring him by force, to issue an arrest warrant. At paragraph 8, on the 4th of May, 2004, regional and international arrest warrants were issued against Mr. Boskoski. According to the investigative judge in relation to the interview conducted by the investigative judge subsequently in Croatia last year, Mr. Boskoski stated that he left to that -- on the 1st of May, 2004. Your Honours, but you'll note in the Defence motion that Mr. Boskoski states to this Court that he left Macedonia on the 30th of April, 2004, which is the same date that he received the summons to attend the following day. The -- the Macedonian authorities were asked this particular question: Whether or not Mr. Boskoski was obliged to present himself to the court or police authorities on the basis of the summons and the investigation, and the investigative judge said no, he was not obliged to report to the police or the courts, however, he was obliged to appear before the investigative judge on the 1st of May because he received a summons as an accused, he was also informed why he had been summonsed, he was informed of his rights and consequences of his failure to appear before the investigating judge. Your Honour, the Prosecution submits that those facts clearly show that Mr. Boskoski left Macedonia to avoid Prosecution for those particular crimes. Obviously it would be more difficult for Mr. Boskoski to be prosecuted for those crimes outside the jurisdiction of Macedonia. Your Honour, this is also supported by the attachment to the Prosecution's motion on the 7th of June, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, while you are still on the -- before you are leaving this document, the top of the page, the so-called summary translation, first line reads Document Reference, second line, number 504/05 dated 28 April, 1005. So that is another mistake that there is on this document. I mean, in the meantime, another thousand years have passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We apologise for that and a complete, accurate version --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go to tab 7 now because I think that's what you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we go to -- not tab 7 for the new bundle but this is in relation to the annex D to the Prosecutor's response on the 7th of June, but we actually have it on the screen now, Your Honours. This is Mr. Boskoski's response to the investigative Judge in Croatia, where he was subsequently arrested, stating that -- he explained -- he explained to the judge he left Macedonia after he received information from police officers about an order they had received to take him to the border between Macedonia and Serbia and liquidate him. Namely, the mandate and the immunity commission lifted his immunity, and after that he left the republic urgently. That's an admission by Mr. Boskoski to the investigative judge in Croatia that he was aware that judicial proceedings were issued against him, and he discovered that fact obviously by the summons that he received or his lawyers received on the 30th of April, but also through police officers. And it's clear that Mr. Boskoski was not -- was not liquidated at the border but was assisted by the police to leave -- by certain police, to leave the country. The Prosecution's submission would be that if it was the case that Mr. Boskoski was in serious threat of his life, that would have been put forward in the Defence motion. However, we ask Your Honours not to accept that to be -- to be a fact. And, Your Honour, this again is further supported by another admission by Mr. Boskoski that he intended to escape prosecution in Macedonia by interview that was conducted with the SBS Dateline programme. It is an Australian current affairs programme which was conducted which Mr. Boskoski whilst he was at large in Croatia last year. And this is an attachment, Annex G, to the motion of the 7th of June, the response to the Defence motion on the 7th of June. And you'll see it on Sanction now. He's being interviewed about the Rashtanski Lozja case. And he states: "They knew they had to apply pressure by taking away my immunity. They concocted a trial so that I'd escaped across the border so that I'd either be caught or eliminated at the border. I received information about their plans and those who were supposed to do this to me, and they let me go, and illegally --" he's quite aware that it was not legal to leave -- "and illegally took me across the border, the Macedonia-Serbian border, and I came... secretly into Croatia. I haven't escaped, I'm still in Macedonia ..." In fact, he was in Croatia at the time. Your Honour, the Prosecution would ask that you accept that it's not credible that Mr. Boskoski's life was at stake when he left Macedonia. We ask you to accept that he left Macedonia to avoid prosecution in those matters. And we ask you to accept that there's a high likelihood that if Mr. Boskoski is released, provisionally released from these proceedings, there's a high likelihood that he would do exactly the same thing again, as Mr. Boskoski now is not just facing one set of charges in this court but two sets, one in the Croatian courts, which it's submitted gives him twice the motive to flee like he did in the first instance. Mr. Boskoski remained at large for about four months in -- in Macedonia -- in Croatia, and he was subsequently arrested by the Croatian authorities in August last year. So not only did he flee, he actively stayed away from the Prosecution in Macedonia when he was legally obliged. He knew that there were regional and international warrants out against him and an obligation to answer the charges, he did not. He was in blatant disregard of those court orders. As far as his general incentive to flee should he be provisionally released, the charges in Croatia are serious, of course, and that is one incentive that was incentive for him to flee before. Also, I think the Defence slightly minimised the seriousness of the charges that he appears before you -- that he appears for here today. He's charged with failing to punish subordinates for -- for the killing of seven civilians in Ljuboten village, the destruction of a number of houses, and also the cruel treatment of up to a hundred Ljuboten residents. The Prosecution submits that a -- unlike the Defence's submission that no prison sentence would flow from that, that certainly a substantial prison sentence would flow from that. As far as whether he would be a danger to victim witnesses or other people, placing him back into the same community where the victims and witnesses in fact live back in Macedonia inevitably increases the opportunity for the accused to have influence over Prosecution witnesses. In a lot of cases before the Tribunal, many of the accused are provisionally released to areas in which the victims and witnesses do not live. The problem in Macedonia is exacerbated by the fact that the victims and witnesses live in the same area as the accused. As the accused has received extensive disclosure in these matters, obviously the identity of victims and witnesses are known. If the allegations in the Rashtanski Lozja case are correct, obviously Mr. Boskoski has the inclination to act illegally and we would submit that it would support the possibility that he may interfere with victims and witnesses. I think his ability to -- to influence the legal process can be seen in the fact that police assisted him to leave -- on Mr. Boskoski's account, police assisted him to leave Macedonia and enter Croatia, knowing that proceedings were being issued against him. And I ask Your Honours to take note of the confidential Annex A, confidential Annex part A, Annex A to the witness protection motion of the Prosecution filed on the 27th of April relating to the significant support that Mr. Boskoski, and for that matter Mr. Tarculovski, has in Macedonia. As far as the length of time to trial, it's clear that the longer the time between the -- the longer of the detention before the trial date may favour provisional release rather than a shorter time period. There are indications, Your Honour - I'm not sure whether you are aware - there are indications that this trial may in fact go to trial at an earlier time than is envisaged by the Defence. There are a number large cases scheduled to commence but this case, I believe, is maybe one of the first cases to fill in if one of those cases can't proceed. If -- if that is true, that the trial date is shorter rather than longer, bearing in mind the -- Mr. Boskoski's prior conduct in avoiding the Prosecution for the Rashtanski Lozja case, it's the Prosecution's submission that it would be not -- not a -- not a beneficial decision to -- to allow that risk to occur for a short period of time if the trial is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in fact going to commence. In relation to the guarantees, Your Honours, as far as the Croatian government is concerned in relation to this case, the Prosecution believe that the Croatian government have acted in good faith in relation to this case. As far as the Croatian government's or the Croatian court's view of the matter, their view is and has been for the last seven months, since Mr. Boskoski's been in custody before being transferred to the Tribunal, that he is a flight risk. It was their view that if he was released or on provisional release, he would -- he would leave Croatia, which is why the detention order was in place. However, the president of the court believes that risk is no longer there but the state prosecution office in -- the state attorney's office in Croatia have said that they would be applying for his detention if he is released back from this Tribunal. As far as the Macedonian government guarantees are concerned, Your Honours, the Prosecution believe that the Macedonian government have been acting in good faith in relation to this investigation and others. The relationship has been good at a political and executive level. Functionaries within the Macedonian government have been very cooperative. Obviously, the difficulty exists in the political and executive level to be able to control what actually happens on the ground. Clearly in relation to the fleeing of Mr. Boskoski from Macedonia to Croatia last year, on Mr. Boskoski's own admissions some police from the Macedonian government assisted him, and obviously all it needs to be is a few and the guarantees cannot be -- cannot be delivered. But as far as the good faith of the Macedonian government, the Prosecution has no contention with that. One matter that perhaps we should raise is that Mr. Boskoski, as the ex-minister of interior in Macedonia and his want to continue political life there, has significant power and influence in Macedonian society, and we ask Your Honours to accept that it's slightly more difficult for a government to execute arrest of a powerful individual and figure -- figure rather than someone that has less of a significant position in -- in government. This point was raised in the Mrksic decision on appeal against refusal to grant provisional release in October 2002. In relation to Mr. Boskoski, Your Honour, and Mr. Tarculovski I will be shorter, we have no further submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Apostolski -- or, rather, before -- I'll give you the floor to respond to any of the points that have just been made, particularly to what I invited you to address earlier on, and this very last area that has been covered by counsel for the Prosecution, and my question to you is the following: That if your client's prior statements that we have seen on the monitor are correct, and in other words, if it is true that the way that the -- his government, his own government, was acting and his regard was sort of a persecution which involved also a risk to his own life, and we're talking of a relatively short time ago, not much, long time ago, I assume they're still the same government, why would he want to return to Macedonia out -- out of all places?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And Judge Eser, who is the Pre-Trial Judge in this case, would also like to add another question of his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We have heard that Mr. Boskoski is citizen both of Macedonia and of Croatia, and we got a guarantee from the side from Macedonia. We had some declarations from Croatia, from the judiciary, but no -- so far no guarantee from the Croatian government. Could you perhaps also address this point, in particular also the question what would -- if Boskoski, Mr. Boskoski, would -- would be released to Macedonia, what would be the impact on the criminal proceeding which is going on in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: I will come to that, Mr. President, Your Honours. Concerning first question about being -- about his leaving Macedonia and reasons to do so, I will explain shortly. Ljube Boskoski is a member of the parliament. He is now and he was in the April and May 2004 as well. He is member of the oppositional political party in the government -- in the parliament, and there have been some old animosities between him and one member of the government, which was -- who was participating the government in the April and May 2004. Therefore, Ljube Boskoski was not intending to be subject of political prosecution against him. He was afraid that lot of evidence would be fabricated against him, and there is a real danger for him not to face a fair trial in Macedonia. Therefore, he legally leave Macedonia using his diplomatic passport. He legally entered Croatia. He reported to the Croatian authorities. He stay in liberty in Croatia for four months, having day-to-day contact with Croatian authorities regarding issues of Rashtanski Lozja case, and he voluntarily surrendered to Croatian authorities in relating to his charges of Rashtanski Lozja case. The point is, when he left Macedonia there has no -- there has not been indictment against him, there has not been court decision for detaining him. And it is not true that the summary has been given to him at all. At the moment he left Macedonia, he was a free man, having some fear for his life because he has been informed by the relevant -- relevant members of the security that his life might be in danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's make -- get this clear. At the time he left Macedonia, legally or illegally, I don't want to get into that, was he a minister at that time or was he then already in opposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Ljube was in opposition at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the time, so the person with whom he was in conflict, I assume, the other person was then a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you talking about the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that minister still there now and does he still occupy the office of minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: I was just coming to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: In November 2004 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Great minds think alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: In the November 2004, the whole Macedonian government resigned. After the resignment of the government, Mr. Ljube Boskoski, from the Pula Detention Unit, has immediately filed a written request, three written requests to Pula court authorities to be transferred to Macedonia since there has been significant changes in the fairness of the procedure. Since there has been some -- some -- there has been new personal government orchestra. Therefore, he asked to be transferred to Macedonia. It is the greatest argument that he never really wanted to escape facing charges. The point is he wanted to be sure that he would face fair trial in Macedonia. That is the case in -- for Ljube Boskoski. And the question of -- the second question was about -- please can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was you so far have only dealt with the situation in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: What is the reaction by the Croatian judiciary? Because you know we have heard that Mr. Boskoski's also prosecuted in Croatia, and so far we do not have some sort of government guarantee from the side of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. We do not have written guarantees from Croatian authorities, but instead, in the Prosecution's response in Confidential Annex C, paragraph 7, Croatian authorities have stated that Republic of Croatia does not intend to stipulate a provisional release of the indictee from the supervision of Croatian authorities in order to finish the proceeding in Rashtanski Lozja case as the Republic of Croatia respects the presidency of the ICTY and has no objection for the proceedings to continue after the proceedings before this Tribunal. And in 7(B), they -- they leave an option that if Court, by the way decides Mr. Ljube Boskoski to be provisionally released in Croatia, that he would act accordingly as they did in the cases of other indictees that were provisionally released in Croatia since that Republic of Croatia has long history of dealing with this such situations. So that would be my address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I now give the floor to Mr. Apostolski on behalf of accused Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, respected colleague Prosecutor, the motion for a provisional release has been filed on the submission of the evaluation of the real possibilities and uncontested facts. We believe that our case is strong, real, and justified. As the Defence declared in the motion for provisional release, the accused fulfils the conditions required by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the Tribunal. The accused guarantees to be accessible for the trial and would not pose a danger for any victims, witnesses, or other persons. Regarding the issue of the seriousness of the criminal charges that he is charged for, that the accused Tarculovski is charged, we want to stress that for more serious acts against humanity, serious violations of the Geneva Conventions in the cases the Prosecutor versus Haradinaj and allies, the Prosecutor versus Milutinovic and allies, the Prosecutor against Prlic and others, they were released. They were provisionally released. As the Court knows, the accused Johan Tarculovski has never refused to cooperate with the Tribunal. By the mistake of the authorities of the Republic of Macedonia, he has unfortunately been arrested and detained without being previously notified or given a chance to voluntarily surrender to the Tribunal. It is a fact that Johan has never received a summons or in any way notified that against him an indictment has been placed. The manner of his arrest we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here for a moment, because I recall, in preparing for today's sitting, I recall reading somewhere a statement by the Prosecution that your client knew of the existence of an indictment against him quite some time -- quite some time ago, and he let practically years pass before he even again reacted to the approaches that the Office of the Prosecutor was trying to make in his regard. So I would like you to address that, because I remember reading it somewhere. So it's not a question of -- of all of a sudden as if this fell from Heaven and hit him on his head and suddenly he found himself here and now he is complaining that he was never given a chance to voluntarily surrender. It seems to me from what I have read, if what I have read is correct, of course, because then that stands to be seen, that he knew from quite some time ago that he was not only a suspect but also an indicted person, and he decided for reasons of his own, which may be good or may be bad, to try and avoid finding himself here. I'm not suggesting that he tried to escape or anything of this sort, but he just reacted passively at a certain point in time. And that is something that I think you need to address, or at least that we would like to hear some submissions about.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted in the continuation of my presentation to address this question. The accused Johan Tarculovski has been informed by telephone and called to appear for an interview. The telephone information, according to Macedonian law, is not a valid summons for hearing. The only valid manner to call someone for interview is by written summons which should be personally delivered to the person. I want to address -- I'm addressing the procedure when he was called for an interview. And after the indictment has been raised, he couldn't even assume that there is an indictment against him. So neither the accused nor -- he was not -- neither able nor aware that an indictment has been filed against him before the Tribunal in The Hague. By the way, the accused accepts full cooperation with the Court Tribunal, including being interviewed by the Prosecution in accordance with Article 63, 42 and 43 of the Rules. Was my explanation sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that is your explanation, we are not going to tell you whether it's sufficient or not. I mean, that's your explanation. We'll tell you when we hand down our decision. So -- and you also have to hear what the Prosecution has to say on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Macedonia guarantees that if Johan is provisionally released, he will be at the disposal to the Tribunal. As all said by our minister of justice, the Macedonian government in the past has practically showed that it cooperates with The Hague Tribunal even though there is no law for cooperation with the Tribunal. Macedonia created conditions for unobstructed work of the Tribunal and has given at their disposal all the classified and secure documents to the Office of the Prosecutor by the state. Also, by the request of the Prosecutor, interviews were held with top intelligence structures and even some witnesses were arrested who avoided to face the Tribunal. The cooperation with the Tribunal is a top priority of the Macedonian government, which has established a Commission for Cooperation consisting of the top ministers, including the minister of justice, the minister of interior, and the minister of foreign affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You don't need to address that much, because basically it's conceded by the Prosecution. In other words, it supersedes any other statement by the Prosecution that we may have received in the written documentation, written pleadings pertaining to this issue. So there is no reason why we should even waste --

utterances.speaker: MR. APOSTOLSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to address this issue with one question -- with one sentence. Your Honour, the accused is not connected to any case of influencing witnesses or has ever tried to contact any of the victims from the intensive terrorist attacks from 2001 until the day of his arrest. Johan Tarculovski has never been prosecuted criminally. Neither there is a proceeding against him at the moment. For these facts we have provided evidence to the Court, records from the criminal evidence, criminal records of Johan Tarculovski held -- kept within the Ministry of Interior as well as an affidavit of the competent courts in the Republic of Macedonia. In Macedonia, unlike the other countries of former Yugoslavia, there is no single case of intimidation of witnesses, so the courts should not fear that if the accused Johan Tarculovski is provisionally released will intimidate witnesses or in any other way influence on them. His clean past is a further confirmation of this fact. Furthermore that on 19th of May, 2005, the Macedonian parliament has adopted a law for protection of witnesses which regulates the procedure and the conditions of providing protection and assistance to the witnesses, justice collaborators, victims who are appearing as witnesses. After the intensive terrorist attacks of 2001, Johan Tarculovski got happily married and got his first daughter, Melani. Prior to his detention, he lived a happy life. He enjoyed the first days of the life of his daughter. Since his daughter turns 20 days, Johan was arrested and has not seen his daughter since then. I ask the Court to take into consideration the fact that the chances for the commencing of the trial, according to the estimate of the Defence, is difficult to happen before 2007. Even if the Prosecution allocates all the resources needed to expedite the pre-trial filings, the Defence would need considerable amount of time to prepare for the trial. We ask the Courts to have into consideration the -- that all persons are equal before the International Tribunal and that accused should be presumed innocent until proven guilty, which is in accordance to the provision of the Tribunal's Statute. With the permission of the Courts, we submitted a written statement by Johan Tarculovski in which he guarantees that if provisionally released he would appear for trial and would not pose a danger for the victims, witnesses, and the other persons. We respect -- we ask the Court to grant the motion for provisional release of the accused Johan Tarculovski. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Apostolski. Madam Minister, would you like to add anything to what you have previously stated in relation to accused Tarculovski or would you just reiterate?

utterances.speaker: MS. MLADENOVSKA-GJORGJIVESKA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could only add a few sentences. Your Honours, I wish to amend my statement briefly only with issues that I spoke about previously. Actually, the Republic of Macedonia really at this moment many reform processes are under way, and these reform processes are mostly concentrated in the police and in the justice system bodies, the reforms of the justice system. I wish to stress certain figures relevant for the work of the police from the beginning of this year onwards. It has been acted upon 513 warrants issued in the Republic of Macedonia, and these persons have been arrested after the warrants were issued. Observed is a percentage of decrease of crime rate in the overall territory in the state, and that percentage is between 18 and 43 per cent in various parts of the territory of the Republic of Macedonia. It should be noted that the crime rate has significantly decreased in the crisis regions from the conflict of 2001, and in the region of Tetovo, for instance, has decreased by some 40 per cent. This percentage of reduction of the crime rate also goes along with the fact that the process of discovering of the perpetrators of crime, also of the most serious crimes, for instance, from the beginning of the year until the end of June of 2005, in the Republic of Macedonia a total of 22 murders have been committed and only one of these cases has not been clarified. Regarding the others, the perpetrators have been discovered and proceedings against them have been initiated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Honourable Minister. Let me check something. What's the position if at all that certain Ljube Bosk -- sorry, not -- Ljubco Georgievski holds at present within VMRO? Ljubco. He was former Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Ljubco Georgievski was former Prime Minister of Macedonia until 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what is he now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: He's Member of Parliament now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of which party?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VMRO People's Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it the same party which your client belongs to or is part of?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Mr. President, there has been -- the VMRO Party has been recently split in two and I do not know exactly which part of it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But is it the party in government or not? No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: -- opposition

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's in the opposition. Okay. Yes. I think we can safely go back to the Prosecution now for final address on the submissions by Mr. Apostolski, and then you will have the opportunity to reply if you need to, Mr. Apostolski. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a couple of brief points in the beginning. It is a significant one to raise again, namely the possible start date of the trial. Indications, quite real indications have been given to us that this trial may be listed for next year, and obviously that's a significant factor in weighing up the issue of provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This may or may not and -- I've been here for four years now, and I would rather prefer to hear something more concrete and more reliable than may or may -- it's very easy to tell someone, you know, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your doubt, Your Honour. I've been here for a while too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- your case may come up. It depends. So at the present moment, if there is no clear indication that this case is scheduled to start in 2006, we cannot assume that it will start or that it will even probably start in 2006. So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to my friend's submission about there's been no case of witness interference in Macedonia, in the Rashtanski Lozja case, which is the case which obviously Mr. Boskoski is being tried for in Croatia, the four accused have been acquitted in Macedonia and the Prosecution are appealing that case right at the moment on the basis that the verdict was assessed as a series of failures and it's not comprehensive and contradictory, so that's in the process at the moment. The -- from Annex F, which is a newspaper report from a number of newspapers in Macedonia to the Prosecution motion of the 7th of June, in the last paragraph Your Honours will see that, according to the Prosecution, the withdrawal of the main witness's statements in the main hearing took place due to the pressure and threats from the indictees' families and the audience in the court. So it's just a -- it seems to present itself in stark contrast to what's been put forward by my friend. As far as Mr. Tarculovski's ability or likelihood to attend at trial, I think it's clear that the -- the Defence admit or the accused admits that he was contacted by the Prosecution last year in order to be interviewed, and because a summons wasn't given to him he failed to attend. I would like to thank my friend for allowing me to put in a set of facts which relate to the attempts that the Prosecution office has made in the last year to try and contact Mr. Tarculovski before he was arrested in March this year to appear for interview in Macedonia. What Your Honours have before you, I think it's been distributed and perhaps I'll mark it as number 9, is a request for assistance to the Macedonian government to serve summonses on a number of individuals who were unable to be served despite the best efforts of the Prosecution and the Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Justice. In that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's a single document, Your Honour. It's reference number BS/T07/M --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I have made myself a note here before we rise today that you need to tender these two documents formally because they haven't been tendered as yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we need to have them on the record, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In that request for assistance, the Prosecution lay down the basis for asking further attempts to be made by the Macedonian government to try and find Mr. Tarculovski. Consistent with what my friend has said, from -- on the second page you see the attempts that were made in June and early July to try and contact Mr. Tarculovski. They were quite intensive attempts for at least a ten to 15-day period. Summonses were unable to be served on him. The registered address of Mr. Tarculovski was not the address that he lived at. That made the initial serving the summons difficult. And in fact, the Macedonian authorities, the Ministry of Interior, did not know where Mr. Tarculovski in fact resided. This led to a number of contacts with Mr. Tarculovski through some confidential informants, and you'll see from the facts stated in this document that two different sources contacted Mr. Tarculovski and conveyed the message that the Prosecution investigators planned to interview him and he decided not to -- not to attend. And one of the messages came back that Mr. Tarculovski would not attend until he received a summons. The difficulty obviously arose, the fact that Mr. Tarculovski would not say where in fact he lived. After a number of attempts were made to locate him, the phone number of Mr. Tarculovski was provided. He was spoken to by an investigator. He said that he would attend, and that -- two days later, and he didn't do so. Then in July, you can see that the mobile phone was then sold to another person, and that other person didn't -- the SIM card, and that other person wasn't able to say where Mr. Tarculovski was. The Prosecution would submit that the selling of the -- or the giving away of the SIM card right at the time when the Prosecution were intensively trying to contact Mr. Tarculovski is certainly some act of -- act of avoidance of cooperating with the Tribunal. This -- this avoidance of speaking to Prosecution investigators led to Mr. Tarculovski's arrest in October 2004, arrest for interview, and also led to his subsequent arrest in March. The Prosecution did not feel it was appropriate to summons him after the act of avoidance in the past. As far as Mr. Tarculovski's incentive to flee, his prior behaviour, the Prosecution submits, shows that. Also the charges that Mr. Tarculovski are facing are very serious. He has been alleged by the Prosecution to be the main instigator in the killings of seven people, the destruction of a large number of properties in a village, and the cruel treatment of ten people from that village. He was the leader, on the Prosecution's allegations, of the group that committed the ground attack on Ljuboten village, which was largely against a civilian population. If Mr. Tarculovski is found guilty of these offences, the Prosecution's submission would be that the prison sentence would be quite lengthy. As far as -- obviously the Defence have raised in their motions that he has no means to flee. It's clear from the documents that his family is receiving substantial funding, and he also has vehicles, et cetera, in which to do so if it was his -- if that was his position. As far as whether he poses a danger to victims, witnesses, or other people, the fact of his involvement in the Ljuboten event, the Prosecution would submit he is a violent individual. The Prosecution initially thought that the accused had a prior criminal record for a violence offence but it appears it wasn't a criminal record but a misdemeanour proceedings which has -- his slate has been wiped clean. The difficulty again arises that if Mr. Tarculovski is released, he will be placed back -- right back into the community of where the victims and witnesses in fact live, and that in itself, Your Honours, the Prosecution submit, poses a danger to victims. It creates possibilities for intimidation to occur, and I'd like to refer Your Honours to the decision of Delalic on the 24th of October, 1996, in the decision on the motion for provisional release filed by the accused Hazim Delic. "The Court held that relevant to this determination is the fact the accused wishes upon his release, in return -- to return to the location where the alleged crimes took place. For instance, a mere presence of an accused convicted for murder in the vicinity of victims and witnesses may have a substantial impact on them and on their willingness to cooperate with the International Tribunal." That may be the case -- that may be more of a case to -- to not grant provisional release than, say, for other accused who are sent back to other areas. And, Your Honours, the Prosecution ask Your Honours to take note of the witness -- the security situation in Macedonia in relation to the annex for the Prosecution's motion for protection measures for victims and witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. And it is precisely to this last intelligence report that we have -- that is of some concern to us that I'm going to address the two parties now, and I will ask for reaction from the Defence counsel in particular to what I'm going to say. Intelligence report that we have, Mr. Godzo, in relation to your client speak of a demonstration which occurred on the 18th of March of this year in the town of Tetovo. This was allegedly a demonstration held to -- in favour of your client but in protest to the missing person issue that, as you know about, and also and his support in relation to the Rashtanski Lozja case. It is reported to us that the family of your client participated in this demonstration, and it is also reported to us that during this demonstration anti-ICTY posters were shown, and the ICTY indictment was actually also mentioned. Then there was -- that was on the 18th of March. On the 22nd of March, then, there seems to have been another demonstration, this time in support of your client but also in support of accused Tarculovski, and incidentally, this was held, out of all places, right in front of the Supreme Court building in Skopje. It is reported to us that afterwards this -- first of all, that this consisted of about 1.500 demonstrators, some of whom then continued their march towards the parliament building. The information that we have is that this was not a spontaneous demonstration at all but that it had all the givings, all the markings of an organised demonstration, with demonstrators being pulled, brought over from outside Skopje. There were banners. And we are also told that ultimately this was a peaceful demonstration. But we are also told, and this is particularly more relevant to your client, Mr. Apostolski, than to Mr. Boskoski, that in this peaceful demonstration of the 22nd of March, 2005, in Skopje, so-called football fans from a committee participated during the demonstration. We are told that your client was head of this formation in the past. The information that we have is that formation has been described as violent in the past, and we are also informed that during the demonstration calls for weapons and ammunition were heard in support of your client. With regard to your client Mr. Boskoski, and in relation to this 22nd March demonstration in Skopje, we are informed that a substantial part of the supporters, demonstrators supporting -- showing support for your client came from the so-called Lions formation, better described to us as an ex-special police formation composed of police reservists and founded by your client way back in 2001 and affiliated to him. We are also told that this was disbanded, this formation was disbanded by the Ministry of Interior after your client resigned, and the reason for the disbanding of -- disbandment of this formation was because of the severe and serious incidents that this unit was supposed to be involved in. I don't think I need to say any more. What I have said is self-explanatory and justifies on a prima facie basis, of course, the concerns that we have in relation to both applications for provisional release, because notwithstanding the certainty that the Trial Chamber has on the guarantees offered by the government of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia, we still have to deal with these problems. So I now give you the floor, then you. And I also want a confirmation from the Prosecution whether the information that we have is correct or not, because ultimately, I mean, you may have checked yourself and come to a different conclusion, and whether these are of concern to you as well because no one has mentioned. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will address to the Trial Chamber referring your questions. Addressing the meeting in Tetovo on 18th of March, as I have heard. Well, that meeting was not organised by any organisation to support any political idea. It was spontaneous meeting of the citizens of village of Celopek, which is the village where Mr. Boskoski was born. It is near Tetovo. The meeting held place in the Tetovo main square, and it was not as -- there were not so many participants in the meeting because it is not a big village. The village of Celopek is a small village. But mostly in the centre of Tetovo it is a great possibility that many -- there were many spectators, many usual pedestrians in the street. The point is that Mr. Ljube Boskoski has nothing to do in organising any protest against this Tribunal. He has shown by now his -- the great respect for this Tribunal, and his commitment for the international rule of law is very huge. During the time he was minister of interior in Republic of Macedonia, he has personally started the cooperation with this Tribunal regarding possible -- possible incidents and possible charges that occurred during the events in 2001. Therefore, meeting in Tetovo in 18th of March, by my opinion and his opinion, I think, has nothing to do with him. He has not any part taken in the organisation of that meeting. And the other issue is meeting in Skopje on 22nd of March before the Supreme Court. Even less my opinion is that meeting before the Supreme Court was not addressed to these proceedings. Either it was not addressed to Ljube Boskoski's support. I do not have the information about the both of the meetings. Officially I have never received such information. But as a Macedonian citizen, as a part of my knowledge, the meeting before the Supreme Court of Skopje, it was mainly addressed to the Rashtanski Lozja case. It was -- yes. It is different case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point that I was trying to make is that these two instances, these two demonstrations, albeit that your clients were not directly involved in the organisation - I'm not suggesting that they were - but the fact that these two demonstrations took place, if they indeed did take place, is indicative that they still enjoy quite a support in the Republic of Macedonia. So -- and support by certain quarters, particularly in regard to your client, this Lions unit that has been disbanded precisely because of its past. So this is what I need you to address.

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: I will address now, Mr. President. Well, the point is that since my assignment in this case, I am aware that it is -- all the -- all the issues regarding this case have been monitored by this Tribunal, but I have never ever -- I can never recall to any demonstration which has been organised since I have been assigned. There has been no other public demonstrations against this -- this Tribunal. Not at all, Mr. President. Never in Macedonia. Macedonian people strongly believe in the justice of this Tribunal and international rule of law. So there is not any need to demonstrate against the institution in which they believe. And the Lions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Godzo, let's not confuse issues. I am more aware than you may think that I am that the former Republic of Macedonia was amongst the first ex-Yugoslav republics to be admitted, together with Slovenia, in the Council of Europe, to have a judge, a friend of mine in the European Court of Human Rights, representation in the International Association of Judges. So the question of the democracy and guarantees from the political -- from the political set-up in Macedonia is not -- is not an issue. It's the question we don't doubt for a moment whether Macedonia believes in the rule of law. Of course it does. Otherwise, it wouldn't be respected the way it is amongst the Committee of Nations. So that's not -- not an issue. The question is not whether in Macedonia there has been any kind of governmentally or politically organised demonstrations against the ICTY. That's not an issue. But I am, together with my two Judges, colleagues, we are told from intelligence gathering that we receive that in the 18th March demonstration in Tetovo, the place where you -- near where your client was born, in this what you describe as a spontaneous demonstration --

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Yes, yes, meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- they had spontaneous posters against the Tribunal, and I have learnt from my political past that spontaneous placards and spontaneous posters do not fall from Heaven. They are made available beforehand. So what is spontaneous does not really remain spontaneous. Spontaneous is the idea, maybe, but what follows up is not spontaneous. So is -- do you have anything else to tell us in relation to these two points?

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. Fine. THE ACCUSED BOSKOSKI: [Interpretation] Sorry, I was not able to hear these --

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: -- express what he was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have a system here where there is a distance between counsel and client, and if you need to consult with your client, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: I know what his point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I haven't received interpretation. I don't know what he said. Is it something that the Tribunal needs to hear or is it something that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GODZO
utterances.text: Yes, shortly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.
